--- Page 39 ---
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(s).      OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO(s).34586/2025)
STATE OF ODISHA & ORS.                      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
CHHABINDRA KUMAR SAMAL                      RESPONDENT(S)
(along with other connected matters as per the Record of
Proceedings)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellants assail the impugned orders passed by
the learned Division Bench and the learned Single Judge
of the High Court of Orissa at Cuttack, allowing the Writ
Petitions  preferred  by  the  respondents,  who  are
contractual pharmacists in the Mobile Health Unit/Team in
the medical facilities provided under the National Rural
Health Mission (NRHM).
3. The learned Single Judge allowed the transferred
Original Application(s)/Writ Petition(s), directing the
appellants to consider the case of the Writ Petitioners
in view of the directions given by this Court in “ The
State of Odisha & Ors. vs. Amit Kumar Mishra & Ors.1”
1  S.L.P. (C.) No.13077/2020
1

--- Page 40 ---
4. In the matter of Amit Kumar Mishra (supra), this Court
interpreted  the  provisions  contained  in  the  Odisha
Pharmacist Service (Methods of Recruitment and Conditions
of Service Rules), 2015, particularly Rules 4 and 6
thereof, to hold that under Rule 4, the contractual
pharmacists are to be absorbed once they have completed
six (06) years of satisfactory contractual service, and
the contractual pharmacists who are yet to complete six
(06) years of contractual service are to be deemed to be
contractual Government employees and would be regularised
as and when they complete six (06) years of satisfactory
service, as per the proviso.
5. This Court further observed that, in view of the
aforesaid,  there  is  little  doubt  that,  as  per  the
statutory rules, the State of Odisha itself has provided
for a deeming provision for such contractual employees,
namely, pharmacists. Rule 5 of the said rules speaks
about modalities for induction of the pharmacists in the
cadre, while Rule 6 mentions the method of recruitment.
6. In view of the Rule position, this Court refused to
interfere with the similar directions issued by the High
Court in the matter of Amit Kumar Mishra (supra). In the
present batch of Writ Petitions, the High Court followed
its earlier order(s) in Amit Kumar Mishra (supra), as
approved by this Court.
2

--- Page 41 ---
7.  Mr.  K.M.  Nataraj,  learned  Additional  Solicitor
General, appearing for the appellants, submitted that
sub-rule (1) of Rule 4 of the Odisha Pharmacist Service
(Methods of Recruitment & Conditions of Service) Rules
2019 (for short, “the 2019 Rules”), has been further
amended by the Odisha Pharmacist Service (Method of
Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Amendment Rules,
2020, notified in the Odisha Gazette on 27 th  November
2020. The said amendment reads as under:
“  2.  In  the  Odisha  Pharmacist  Service  (Methods  of
Recruitment  and  Conditions  of  Service)  Rules,  2019
(hereinafter referred to as the said Rules), in Rule 4,
for Sub-rule (1) excluding the provisos, the following
sub-rule shall be substituted, namely:—
(1) On the date of commencement of these Rules, all the
contractual Pharmacists, who have been duly recruited by
the  concerned  Societies  or  Schemes  for  working  in
different fixed Healthcare Facilities only against the
posts approved or sanctioned by the Government in the
Programme Implementation Plan (PIP) or Action plan of
concerned Society or Scheme and have completed (06)
years  of  satisfactory  contractual  service,  shall  be
deemed to be regular Government employees as one time
measure subject to fulfillment of eligibility criteria
as prescribed under Rule 5. ”
8. Basing on the above amendment, it is argued that the
contractual pharmacists working only in fixed healthcare
facilities  are  entitled  for  consideration  for
regularisation upon completion of six (06) years of
3

--- Page 42 ---
contractual service. Therefore, the respondents, having
worked in Mobile Health Units/Teams, would not be covered
within the sweep of the mandate of sub-rule (1) of Rule 4
of the 2019 Rules, as amended, and hence, the order
passed by the High Court, in view of the amendment in the
Rules, is not correctly interpreting the present rule
position.
9. It is also argued that the Writ Petitioners, having
not  challenged  the  validity  of  the  Rules,  are  not
entitled for any relief, as the Rules, framed under
Article 309 of the Constitution, have statutory force,
and any direction by the High Court contrary to the Rules
is not permissible.
10. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondents/writ
petitioners would submit that the High Court has taken a
correct view in light of the law laid down by this Court
in Amit Kumar Mishra (supra). It is submitted that the
rule position, as it existed before 27 th  November 2020,
did  not  make  any  difference  between  contractual
pharmacists employed in a fixed healthcare facility and
those who are employed in the Mobile Health Unit/Team.
11. Learned counsel for the respondents would submit that
reading the amendment to be applicable to the existing
contractual pharmacists working in the Mobile Health
Unit/Team would be contrary to the law laid down by this
Court in Amit Kumar Mishra (supra).
4

--- Page 43 ---
12. Having heard learned counsel for the parties, we are
of the considered view that the amendment made in sub-
rule (1) of Rule 4 of the 2019 Rules would operate
prospectively and would not take away the rights accrued
in  favour  of  any  contractual  pharmacist,  be  it  a
pharmacist working in a fixed healthcare facility or one
working in the Mobile Health Unit/Team.
13. Reading it differently would unsettle the law laid
down by this Court in Amit Kumar Mishra (supra). It is
settled that unless the legislature or the rule-making
authority makes a particular rule retrospective by making
specific provision in that regard, the rules should be
operative prospectively only.
14.  Admittedly,  the  respondents/writ  petitioners  had
completed  six  (06)  years  of  contractual  service  as
contractual pharmacists in the Mobile Health Unit/Team
prior to the amendment dated 27th November 2020. Thus, any
right  which  had  already  accrued  in  favour  of  the
respondents/writ petitioners prior to coming into force
of the amendment to the 2019 Rules, cannot be taken away
by reading the same to be retrospective in effect, when
the Rules do not say so.
15. In  view  of  the  above,  we  are  not  inclined  to
interfere with the impugned orders passed by the High
Court. However, it is made clear that such contractual
pharmacists working in the Mobile Health Unit/Team who
5

--- Page 44 ---
had not completed six (06) years of contractual service
as on 27 th November 2020 shall be governed under the
amendment dated 27th November 2020.
16. The appeals are disposed of in the above terms.
17. Pending  applications,  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.
......................J.
   (PRASHANT KUMAR MISHRA)
......................J.
    (SHREE CHANDRASHEKHAR)

CIVIL APPEAL No.6094/2016 & CIVIL APPEAL Nos.6084-6093/2016
1. Order dated 28 th November, 2016 was passed on these appeals to
the following effect:-
“For the interim measure, the State as well as the appellants
agree that the ends of justice would be met for the time being by
permitting all the candidates who secure equal to or more than
104.51 marks in the preliminary examination (irrespective of the
category to which candidates belong) be permitted to appear in
the final examination without prejudice to the rights of the parties
and  the  various  question  of  law  arising  in  the  appeals.  The
respondents are permitted to complete the process of selection of
Patwaris in accordance with law.”
2. It  is  not  in  dispute that the appellants  participated  in the final
examination pursuant to such order. However, for want of instructions,
learned counsel appearing for the appellants is not in a position to apprise
this Court whether they were selected or not.
3. Be that as it may, since the appellants’ grievance was taken care of
by this Court by the aforesaid interim order and they were permitted to
2

--- Page 66 ---
participate in the final examination, nothing further survives for decision
on these appeals.
4. We hold that the appeals, due to subsequent events and by passage
of time have been rendered infructuous.
5. Accordingly, the appeals stand disposed of as such.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
Civil Appeal No.      /2026 @ SLP(C) No. 21663/2018 & Civil Appeal
No.      /2026 @  SLP(C) No. 21910/2018
1. Leave granted.
2. While disposing of intra-court appeals 1 before it, a Division Bench of
the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at Jaipur, passed inter
alia the following order:-
“We  are  inclined  to  interfere  in  the  order  passed  by  Single
Learned Single Judge. Accordingly, judgment of learned Single
Judge 21st October, 2016 is set aside. The relief prayed in the writ
petitions are thus to be granted.
It is, however, a fact that during pendency of the writ petitions,
Main Examination were held thus taking into consideration the
aforesaid, now direction to the RPSC and the State Government is
to analyse the position by first arranging list of the candidates
strictly in consonance to Rule 15 of the Rules of 1999 as well as
the judgment of the Division Bench of this Court in the case of
Hanuman Jat & Ors.(supra). A candidate called beyond 15 times
to the reserve category and has secured position in the Main
as well as in the interview be Examination eliminated/excluded so
that action of the RPSC remains in consonance to Rule 15 of the
Rules of 1999 with least interference in the selection.
Onwards, the RPSC would not deviate from Rule 15 of the Rules
of,1999, rather not only that candidates would not be called more

1. In pursuance of our order dated 10.09.2026, Ms.Aishwaya
Bhati,  learned  Additional  Solicitor  General,  has  taken
instructions, which are reproduced as under :-
“1. It is informed that, pursuant to completion
of the second round of NEET-SS counselling,
1,857 Super Specialty seats are presently lying
vacant, comprising 1,094 DM/M.Ch. seats and 763
DNB-SS seats. A substantial number of these
seats pertain to highly specialised medical and
surgical disciplines.
2.  The  matter  regarding  filling  up  of  the
vacant Super Speciality seats was considered by

--- Page 78 ---
2
the  Ministry  in  consultation  with  NMC  and
MCC/DGIIS.  During  the  hearing  before  this
Hon'ble Court on 10.09.2026, the Ministry had
informed the Hon'ble Court that a Special Stray
Vacancy Round would be conducted. The Hon'ble
Court also requested the Union Government to
reconsider  the  issue  of  reduction  of  the
qualifying percentile, particularly in view of
the  substantial  number  of  vacant  Super
Speciality seats.
3. The matter has since been reconsidered in
consultation with the concerned stakeholders.
In order to ensure that the available Super
Speciality seats do not remain vacant and that
the available training capacity is optimally
utilised,  it  has  been  decided  that  the
qualifying  percentile  for  NEET-SS  may  be
reduced from the existing 50th percentile to
30th percentile for the purpose of the proposed
Special Stray Vacancy Round.
4.  Consequently,  candidates  securing  30th
percentile and above in NEET-SS would become
eligible to participate in the Special Stray
Vacancy  Round.  It  is  estimated  that  such
reduction  would  make  approximately  6,000
additional  candidates  eligible  for
participation. This would provide a candidate
pool of approximately three times the number of
presently  vacant  seats,  i.c.  approximately
6,000 eligible candidates against 1,857 vacant
seats.
5. It is further proposed that the Special
Stray Vacancy Round may be conducted strictly
in  accordance  with  the  existing
principles/rules applicable to a Stray Vacancy

--- Page 79 ---
3
Round, with no provision for upgradation of
candidates who  are already  holding/joined a
seat.  Accordingly, the vacant seats may be
offered only to candidates who have not joined
a  seat  in  the  earlier  rounds  of  NEET-SS
counselling and who become eligible consequent
upon  the  reduction  of  the  qualifying
percentile.
6.  It  may  be  specifically  noted  that  the
provision for upgradation was already available
and was permitted between Round 1 and Round 2
of the present NEET-SS counselling. Candidates
who participated in Round 2 accordingly had the
opportunity  to  seek  upgradation  from  their
Round 1 allotment.
7.  Since  the  academic  session  has  already
commenced  and  a  considerable  period  has
elapsed,  permitting  further  upgradation  of
candidates who have already joined seats may
result in candidates shifting from one Super
Speciality seat to another several months after
commencement  of  the  academic  session.  This
would, in turn, result in the seats vacated
consequent  upon  such  upgradation  becoming
vacant again, necessitating their inclusion in
a further  counselling round  and potentially
leaving such seats unfilled.
8. It was further decided that, in compliance
with the orders of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in
relation to the State of Tamil Nadu and in the
peculiar  circumstances,  the  40  vacant  in-
service seats pertaining to Tamil Nadu would be
reverted  to  the  State  Government  for  the
limited  purpose  of  enabling  the  State  to
conduct  and  complete  its  own  Stray  Vacancy

--- Page 80 ---
4
Round for a period of one (1) week. Any such
seats remaining unfilled after completion of
the  State's  Stray  Vacancy  Round  would
thereafter be added to the pool of vacant seats
available  with  MCC,  and  the  Special  Stray
Vacancy Round in respect of these seats, along
with the other vacant Super Speciality seats,
would be conducted and completed by MCC in two
(2) weeks.”
2. In the facts and circumstances of the case, we accept
the submission of the learned ASG and direct that immediate
steps shall be taken to comply with the position and stand
taken in Paras 6, 7 and 8, as extracted hereinabove.
3. It is made clear that this order is passed in the
facts and circumstances of the present case and is confined
to the State of Tamil Nadu.
4. The timeline, as indicated in the Judgment passed by
this Court in Ashish Ranjan and Others Vs. Union of India
[(2016) 11 SCC 225] is extended till 06.10.2026.
5. In  view  of  above,  the  writ  petition  and  misc.
application are disposed of and the contempt petition is
closed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.                             OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NOS.460-461/2025)
ANIL BHALLA & ANR. ETC.  ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA & ANR ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Respondent No.2 herein approached the appellants for grant of loan of Rs.3
Lakhs during May, 2021 and they promised to refund the same. Accordingly, a
sum of Rs.2,70,000/- was borrowed and same was not refunded in spite of
repeated requests followed by issuance of legal notice. On account of non-
payment, the appellants are said to have threatened the borrower. Hence, a
complaint came to be lodged which was registered on 05.08.2022 for the
offences punishable under Sections 120B, 403, 406, 420, 384 and 511 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC). Subsequently, a compromise was entered into
between the parties on 20.04.2024 and 20.05.2024, whereunder, all the monies
due to appellants, have been repaid by respondent no. 2 and both parties are
said to have burned their hatchet and did not intent to pursue their grievance.
On account of such settlement having entered into, a petition under Section 482
CrPC was filed by the appellants/petitioners (accused) for quashing of the FIR
and proceedings initiated pursuant to it, which came to be dismissed by the
impugned order. Hence, these appeals.
1

--- Page 84 ---
4. A perusal of the impugned order would indicate that appellants have against
them multiple criminal cases. Taking note of this fact and the allegations that
appellants are charging very high interest and had threatened the complainant
and his family members of dire consequences for non-payment, the High Court
refused to exercise the extra-ordinary jurisdiction to quash the proceedings.
Hence, this appeal.
5. Perusal of the settlement agreement would indicate that appellants and
Respondent No.2 have entered into a settlement and particularly with regard to
the present FIR No. 352 dated 05.08.2024, registered by PS Sector 5,
Panchkula. The learned counsel appearing for respondent-complainant would
also admit that said compromise having been entered into between the parties
and  Respondent No.2 has expressed that he is not inclined to continue the
prosecution. However, learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
would vehemently oppose the said settlement contending inter  alia that on
account of appellants-accused having been charging high interest which is
contrary to the statutory bar and having posed the threat to Respondent No.2, it
would embolden the appellants to indulge in similar acts. 
6. Having regard to the aforestated facts and also the fact that there has been
a settlement arrived at between the parties without any force, threat or
coercion and the dispute is purely due to the payment of money and there
being no amount now due by the Respondent No.2 payable to the appellants-
accused, continuation of criminal trial would only be a waste of precious judicial
time. As such, the continuation of criminal proceedings would not be warranted.
Hence, the prayer sought for in the appeal stands allowed. The proceedings
pending against the appellants pursuant to FIR No. 352/2022 dated 05.08.2022
on the file of PS Sector 5, Panchkula, and all proceedings thereunder, stands
quashed. No order as to costs.
2

--- Page 85 ---
7. The appeals are allowed accordingly.
8. Pending application(s), if any, stands consigned to records.

(ARAVIND KUMAR)
..................J.
( VIPUL M. PANCHOLI)
New Delhi;

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. In the transfer petition filed by the wife, we directed
both parties to go for mediation, considering the short
marital life they had and their young age. However, mediation
has failed and even though we had directed the parties to make
a further attempt and also directed the husband, respondent
herein to make a deposit of Rs.6,00,000/-, which was permitted
to be withdrawn by the petitioner-wife, no resolution has been
arrived at.
2

--- Page 90 ---
T.P.(Criminal)  No.182/2025
2. However today, Ms. Uttara Babbar, learned Senior Counsel
appearing for the petitioner-wife and  Mr. Shadan Farasat ,
learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent-husband
submits that despite best efforts, they have not been able to
settle the matter, even with the active intervention of the
learned Senior Counsel appearing for both parties.
3. Mr. Shadan Farasat  submits that since exorbitant sums
were claimed by the petitioner-wife, no settlement could be
reached and the respondent-husband is also concerned with the
maintenance  granted  of  Rs.1  lakh  per  month,  which  is
challenged in the connected SLP.
4. We notice that the marriage was solemnized on 16.02.2021
and they were separated on 27.04.2022, within which period
their cohabitation was limited to a month, immediately after
which  the  respondent  left  for  the  USA  and  later  from
03.12.2021 when the petitioner-wife was taken to the USA.
After she returned to attend her sister's marriage, she has
not gone back to join her husband. There are no children born
from the wedlock.
3

--- Page 91 ---
T.P.(Criminal)  No.182/2025
5. In the above circumstances, we are of the opinion that
the marriage is irretrievably broken down and there is no
point in the parties fighting over trivial issues, which could
put their future lives into jeopardy.
6. In the above circumstances, we are of the opinion that as
permanent alimony the respondent-husband should pay an amount
of Rs.90,00,000/- in full and final settlement of claims
raised by the petitioner-wife with respect to the marriage.
Learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner-wife
submits that the wife’s jewellery, she received from her
family at the time of marriage is still with the respondent-
husband. Learned Senior Counsel for the respondent-husband
submits that as per his instructions, the petitioner-wife had
taken the entire jewellery, when she left the matrimonial home
and if at all there is anything remaining, it will be handed
over within four weeks.
7. We, hence direct the alimony fixed by us to be paid
within four weeks from today and if any jewellery is remaining
with the respondent-husband the same shall also be returned.
If the petitioner-wife refuses to give the bank details to
facilitate the transfer of funds, the respondent-husband shall
be ready with a Demand Draft in the name of the petitioner-
4

--- Page 92 ---
T.P.(Criminal)  No.182/2025
wife on the next date of hearing. The matter shall be posted
after four weeks and in the meanwhile, we direct that all
proceedings between the parties with respect to the marriage,
both  civil  and  criminal,  shall  stand  stayed.  Order  of
maintenance also shall remain stayed till further orders. On
satisfaction of the amounts directed by us, the respondent-
husband would be entitled to file an application invoking
Article 142 of the Constitution of India for dissolution of
the marriage on grounds of irretrievable breakdown.
8. Post the matter on 28.10.2026.

CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026

MANASH PRATIM BORAH ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. In this case the prosecution alleges cheating, criminal breach of trust
and conspiracy in relation to a proposed “Migrant Labour Survey” project
concerning survey work in Assam and North-Eastern States. According to
the complainant, co-accused  Devashish  Vishwakarma  and others
represented that they had contacts and connection with the Government
Agencies and could facilitate allotment of labour survey work in Assam. It
is further alleged that acting upon such representation, the complainant
transferred substantial amounts in relation to the proposed project and
thereafter allotted districts including Barpeta and Cachar. It is alleged
that appellant and co-accused persons induced the complainant to part
with money under assurance of government linked survey projects.
1                                                                                       SLP(CRL.) NO.10317 OF 2026

--- Page 99 ---
According, to the compliant, despite payment of large amounts they
promised project work, which was not properly executed and disputes
subsequently arose regarding execution and refund of money.
4. Hence, FIR came to be registered for the offences punishable under
Sections 406, 420 and 120-B Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) by the Police
Station District Charkhi Dadri, Haryana. The prosecution contends that
custodial interrogation of the appellant is necessary in connection with
the investigation for cheating, conspiracy and to trace the money
received by accused. It is alleged that appellant participated in project
coordination activities and financial transactions connected with the
proposed survey project. The prosecution and the complainant oppose
the grant of anticipatory bail on the ground of allegation in the complaint
discloses cognizable offence involving cheating and criminal conspiracy.
Hence, in order to ascertain the appellant’s actual role custodial
interrogation is necessary and same requires to be investigated
thoroughly. Hence, they seek for dismissal of the appeal.
5. This court while issuing notice, had granted interim protection in
favour of the appellant and directed that appellant should cooperate with
the investigation. The learned counsel appearing for the State would
fairly submit that appellant has appeared on three occasions before IO
namely as and when called upon but has not been able to state the
whereabouts of the money received. 
6. In the light of there being no flight risk and the fact that appellant has
appeared before the Investigating Officer (IO), we are of the considered
view that appellant is entitled for grant of anticipatory bail.
2                                                                                       SLP(CRL.) NO.10317 OF 2026

--- Page 100 ---
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside.
Appellant is ordered to be released on anticipatory bail on such terms and
conditions as the IO may deem fit to impose including the condition of
directing the appellant to appear before him as and when called upon and
also on the condition that appellant would appear before the jurisdictional
court on all dates of hearing except when exempted for any specific
reason.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL No.2065/2012
GROUP COMMANDANT CISF & ANR.                APPELLANTS
VERSUS
A.THIRUMALAYANDI                  RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Respondent was a constable of the Central Industrial Security Force 1. He
was removed from service on 04 th February, 2000 on four proved charges, (i)
purchased goods without approval of the Canteen Managing Committee, (ii) did
not  deposit  sale  proceeds,  (iii)  manipulated  cash  bills  and  (iv)  purchased
stationary but did not pay the balance. 
2. Upon the order of removal being challenged before the High Court of
Judicature at Madras 2, it was inter alia held that the finding as regards proof of
charge no.(i) was based on total non-application of mind; insofar as charge no.
(ii) is concerned, it was held that relevant particulars were absent in the charge-
sheet; regarding charge no.(iii), it was held not to be proved; and, only charge
no.(iv) was held to be proved. 
3. Based on proof of charge no.(iv), the High Court further went on to hold
that the punishment of removal would be disproportionate to the gravity of
misconduct alleged to have been committed by the respondent. T o shorten the
1 CISF
2 High Court
1

--- Page 119 ---
litigation, the High Court substituted the punishment of removal from service by
ordering withholding of increment for a period of one year. 
4. The judgment and order of the High Court dated 08 th February, 2010 3
substituting the punishment and ordering reinstatement of the respondent in
service is the subject matter of challenge in this appeal.
5. Though special leave was granted on 06 th February, 2012, the appeal has
been effectively heard only from January, 2026 onwards. In due course of time,
the respondent has attained the age of superannuation and, therefore, there is
no question of his reinstatement in service or to give effect to the punishment
that was imposed by the High Court in substitution of the original punishment of
removal.
6. We have noted that while granting leave, the operation of the impugned
order was stayed by this Court. 
7. The sole question arising for decision, on facts and in the circumstances,
is whether the High Court should have remitted the matter to the disciplinary
authority for ordering a suitable punishment based on proof of charge no.(iv).  
8. Since the respondent has attained the age of superannuation, we had
enquired of Ms. Dave, the learned Additional Solicitor General appearing for the
appellants as to the quantum of emoluments the respondent would have been
entitled had the order of the High Court not been stayed and he were permitted
to be reinstated in service and continued till such superannuation.  
9. Facts and figures have been provided. We have also perused an affidavit
filed by the respondent to the effect that upon his removal from service of the
3 impugned order
2

--- Page 120 ---
CISF, he had never been employed in any government or private establishment
and that he had survived for all these years by cultivating a 1.6 acre piece of
land as well as by dairy farming.  
10. T o put an end to the long pending dispute, we are of the view that a
lumpsum compensation may be awarded to the respondent. Accordingly, this
appeal is disposed of by directing the appellants to pay to the respondent a
consolidated sum of Rs.55,00,000/- (Rupees fifty-five lakh) only towards full and
final settlement of the dues. 
11. Let the aforesaid amount be made over to the respondent within three
months from date. 
12. It is clarified that the impugned order shall, however, not be read as a
precedent for deciding future cases.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

(DIPANKAR DATTA)
...........................................J.
(SHEEL NAGU)
New Delhi;
September 16, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.             OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRL.) NO.6961 OF 2026)
SYED RIZWAN AHMED                          APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF U.P. & ANR.                       RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant, in the instant case, is aggrieved
by the order of the High Court, dated 13.01.2026,
wherein the private complaint and the summoning order
for the offence under Section 500 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860, against Respondent No.2, has been queashed,
in the exercise of inherent power under Section 482 of
the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter,
CrPC,1973), on the ground that the list of prosecution
witness, as mandated under Section 204(2) of the CrPC,
1973, has not been filed. Besides this, it was also
held that the appellant has failed to get any witness
examined under Section 202 of the CrPC, 1973, to show
that his image has been lowered in the estimation of
others. Aggrieved by the same, the appellant is before
1

--- Page 124 ---
us.
3. The  short  question  that  arises  for  our
consideration in this appeal is as to whether the
summoning order is maintainable without complying with
the mandate of sub-section (2) of Section 204 read with
Section 202 of the CrPC, 1973.
4. Upon  hearing  the  appellant-in-person  and  the
learned Senior counsel appearing for the respondents,
we find that Section 204(2) of the CrPC is mandatory in
nature, as it clearly provides that “no summons or
warrant shall be issued against the accused under sub-
section (1) until a list of prosecution witnesses has
been filed”. Since this provision has not been complied
with, consequently, the summons issued will have to be
set aside.
5. Consequently, we grant liberty to the appellant to
file a list of prosecution witnesses and, thereafter,
the Ld. Special Chief Judicial Magistrate (Custom),
Lucknow, is directed to proceed, in accordance with
law, in the light of the observations made hereinabove.
6. In such view of the matter, the impugned order
stands set aside to the extent that it quashes the
private complaint and the quashment of the summoning
order stands confirmed.
7. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed in part with
the aforesaid liberty.
2

--- Page 125 ---
8. Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed
of.
.....................J.
  (M.M. SUNDRESH)
                             .......................J.
  (AUGUSTINE GEORGE MASIH)
NEW DELHI;
SEPTEMBER 9, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.          OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(CRL.) NO.10263 OF 2026)
KOMAL KETULKUMAR CHAUDHARY & ORS.             APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF GUJARAT & ORS.                  RESPONDENT(S)
 O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellants and
learned standing counsel for the first respondent-State
and learned counsel for private respondents.
3. During the course of submissions, it was pointed out
that a sum of Rs.34,00,000/- has been deposited by the
appellants before the Trial Court; that the High Court had
modified the condition for the deposit of Rs.5,00,000/-
every two months. There was a breach of the said condition
as the appellants have not complied with the direction
which was issued on the submission of the appellants for
1

--- Page 139 ---
grant  of  anticipatory  bail.  In  substance,  the  said
condition is assailed in this appeal. 
4. Learned counsel for the appellants submitted that
since the private respondents have filed an application
seeking for withdrawal of the amount of Rs.34,00,000/-
deposited by the appellants before the Trial Court and
further the appellants are cooperating with the trial, the
condition for continuation of deposit of Rs.5,00,000/-
every two months may be deleted.
5. In response to this submission, learned counsel for
the private respondents contented that the balance amount
may be deposited by the appellants and permission may be
granted to prosecute their application pending before the
High Court.
6. In the circumstances, we find that while granting the
relief of anticipatory bail, the High Court was not right
in also directing the appellants herein to deposit a sum
of  Rs.5,00,000/-  every  two  months  as  there  was  a
transaction between the parties and there may be disputed
facts emanating in the said case. 
2

--- Page 140 ---
7. Taking note of the fact that the appellants are
cooperating with the trial, we dispose of this appeal by
deleting the condition imposed on the appellants herein
directing them to deposit a sum of Rs.5,00,000/- every two
months. 
8. All other conditions imposed by the High Court by
order dated 16.10.2024 in R/Criminal Misc. Application
(For Anticipatory Bail) No.17481 of 2024 shall however
remain as they are. 
9. The appeal is allowed and we  set aside the order
passed by the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad dated
14.05.2026 in the aforesaid terms.
10. We also clarify that the private respondents are at
liberty to prosecute their application seeking withdrawal
of  Rs.34,00,000/-  deposited  by  the  appellants  herein
before the High Court.
11. The parties are also at liberty to arrive at a
mediated settlement in the case.
12. We  clarify  that  while  deleting  the  aforesaid
condition regarding deposit, all other conditions imposed
3

--- Page 141 ---
by the High Court by order dated 16.10.2024 while granting
anticipatory bail shall remain as they are.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(s).      OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO(s).15917/2025)
KALI CHARAN                              APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
NARENDER SINGH                           RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  appellant  has  preferred  this  appeal,  laying
challenge to the order passed by the High Court, whereby
the High Court partially remanded the suit to the Trial
Court for trial on a specific issue framed by it.
3. The  Trial  Court  and  the  First  Appellate  Court
concurrently decreed the suit filed by the appellant for
specific  performance,  against  which  the
defendant/respondent  herein  had  preferred  an  appeal
before the High Court.
4. According to the High Court, the Trial Court should
have tried an issue as to whether the appellant was in
the  business  of  lending  loans  on  execution  of  such
agreements to sell, in order to secure repayment of the
amount. The High Court was of the opinion that, had the
issue been framed, the parties would have led evidence to
prove that fact.
5. Having heard learned counsel for the parties, we are
of the considered view that the High Court has failed to
1

--- Page 144 ---
consider the pleadings of the parties so as to reason
that a particular issue was required to be framed. There
is no reference to the pleadings of the parties. In that
light, it was not open for the High Court to have framed
an issue only because it was of the opinion that the
issue was germane to decide the litigation. Under Order
XIV CPC, issues for trial are required to be framed based
on the pleadings made by the parties in the plaint and
the written statement.
6. What the High Court says is that a particular issue
should have been framed and the parties should have been
allowed  to  lead  evidence  to  prove  that  fact.  The
principle of trial of a civil suit is just otherwise, in
as much as, an issue in the suit is required to be framed
based on the pleadings of the parties, whereafter the
parties lead evidence on that issue.
7. It is not that, after a full trial and the first
appeal, the High Court could assume that a particular
issue was required to be framed and then again allow the
parties to lead evidence on the issue, even if the
parties were not at variance while exchanging pleadings
in the Trial Court.
8. In view of the above, the impugned order is set aside
and the second appeal before the High Court is restored
to its original number for its decision on its own
merits.
2

--- Page 145 ---
9. Accordingly, the present appeal is allowed in the
above terms.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
......................J.
   (PRASHANT KUMAR MISHRA)
......................J.
    (SHREE CHANDRASHEKHAR)
NEW DELHI

“1.  The  submission  on  behalf  the

benefit of presumption is available to

the prosecution against the accused.

husband of the deceased is not before us,
and, prima facie, it appears to be a case
of suicide, we are of the view that the
petitioners are entitled for protection
during investigation.
3. Issue notice, returnable in six weeks.

in the event the petitioners are arrested

cooperate in the investigation and make
themselves available for interrogation as

the witnesses or tamper the evidence.”

good reason to discharge the interim protection order
granted earlier.

he  shall  co-operate  in  the  trial/

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.       /2026
[@ SLP (C) NO.27674/2025]
MOHAMMED AKBAR & ORS.                 Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF TELANGANA & ORS.           Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal has been filed having been
aggrieved by the dismissal of the writ petition
filed by the appellants by the High Court seeking a
writ of habeas corpus to declare the custody of the
minor  child  taken  by  the  respondent  No.2-Child
Welfare Committee as illegal. The appellants further
prayed for handing over the custody of minor child
to them. 
3.  The High Court vide the impugned order dated
12.06.2025 held that the appellants could not claim
that the child was under illegal detention, since
the minor child was in the safe custody of the Child
Welfare Committee, as per the framework laid down
under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of
Children) Act, 2015 (for short, ‘the 2015 Act’). It
was further observed that neither the adoption deed
was proper, as per the framework under the 2015 Act,

--- Page 172 ---
2
nor the adoption was through the Central Adoption
Resource Agency (for short, ‘CARA’). 
4. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the appellants and the learned counsel appearing for
the respondents.
5. The action was taken by the State, pursuant to
which the child was taken into the custody of the
respondent  No.2-Child  Welfare  Committee  on  the
suspicion that the minor child was sold to the
appellant Nos.1 and 2 by the appellant No.3, who is
the biological mother of the child.
6. The fact that appellant No.3 is the biological
mother of the child is not in dispute.  We are
inclined to hold the factum of the child being given
by way of adoption by the appellant No. 3, in view
of her inability to take care of the child due to
financial constraints, would ipso facto not lead to
the presumption that the child was sold by her to
the appellant Nos.1 and 2. Further, the child was
taken into custody by the appellant Nos.1 and 2 and
it is not a case where the child was not taken due
care of by the appellant Nos.1 and 2, who are his
adoptive parents.
7. Taking note of the aforesaid facts, we are
inclined to set aside the impugned order dated
12.06.2025 passed by the High Court of Telangana in
Writ Petition No. 15079/2025.

--- Page 173 ---
3
8. Consequently, the concerned respondent No.2-
Child Welfare Committee, Shishu Griha, Hyderabad, is
directed to hand over the custody of child to
appellant Nos.1 and 2.
9. We make it clear that we are not touching upon
the issues pertaining the pending investigation(s)
qua other children who are alleged to have been
trafficked.
10. The appeal stands disposed of, accordingly.
11. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also
stand disposed of.
…………………………………………..J.
[M.M. SUNDRESH]
…………………………………………..J.
[PRASANNA B. VARALE]

enhancement of maintenance to the case of petitioner No.2 –

3. The High Court has confirmed the order of maintenance
as awarded by the trial Court.  The trial Court had awarded
Rs.16,000/- (Rupees Sixteen Thousand only) to petitioner
No.1 – wife (Kusum Rawat) and Rs.8,000/- (Rupees Eight
Thousand only) to petitioner No.2 – daughter (Avani Rawat)
till she attains majority. 
4. Mr. S.Mahendran, learned counsel for the respondent
No.2, submits that  the daughter has  attained majority.
According to him, under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal
Procedure,  1973  (for  short,  ‘Cr.P.C.’)  (corresponding
Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita,
2023), a daughter who has attained majority can claim
maintenance only if it is established that due to physical
or mental abnormality or injury, she is unable to maintain
herself.  The learned counsel does not dispute the fact
that respondent No.2 – husband is employed as a Lecturer in
Government  Inter  College  Himmatnagar,  Jaspur,  District
Udham Singh Nagar, Uttarakhand and his monthly salary is
around Rs.1,25,000/-.
5. Mr. S.Mahendran, learned counsel, relied upon the
judgment of this Court in the case of  Abhilasha v. Parkash
&  Ors. 1 to  contend  that  a  daughter  who  has  attained
1 (2021) 13 SCC 99
2

--- Page 177 ---
majority, unless it is established that due to physical or
mental abnormality or injury, she is unable to maintain
herself, is not entitled to claim any maintenance under
Section 125 of the Cr.P.C. and has to approach the Civil
Court. 
6. Mr. Dharmendra Kumar Sinha, learned counsel appearing
for the petitioner(s), on the other hand, relied upon the
judgment of this Court in the case of Jagdish Jugtawat v.
Manju  Lata  &  Ors. 2 to  contend  that  the  Courts  have
recognized the conjoint reading of Section 125 of the
Cr.P.C. read with the provisions of the Hindu Adoptions and
Maintenance Act, 1956, to award maintenance to daughters
who attained majority.
7. Mr. S. Mahendran, learned counsel, however,  contends
that  the  judgment  in  Jagdish  Jugtawat 2  has  been

of Abhilasha1.  Paragraph 23 thereof, reads as under: 
“23.  The  judgment  of  this  Court  in  Jagdish
Jugtawat  is sheet anchor of the learned counsel
for the appellant. The question which came up for
consideration  before  this  Court  in  Jagdish

judgment which is to the following effect: (SCC
p. 423)
"3. In view of the finding recorded and the
observations made by the learned Single Judge

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No(s).  4282/2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 827/2026)
ABDUL RAHIM @ ELUNDI                                   Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH                           Respondent(s)
                          
O R D E R
Heard Mr. Ravi Kumar, learned counsel for the appellant and
Ms. Prerna Singh, learned counsel for the respondent-State of
Andhra Pradesh. 
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of an order of conviction and
sentence awarded to the appellant upon trial in connection with
Sessions Case No. 655 of 2005 dated 28.06.2006, and confirmed by
the Court of XI Additional District and Sessions Judge (Fast Track
Court), Guntur at Tenali, in Criminal Appeal No. 308 of 2006, by
which, upon conviction, he was sentenced to undergo four years
rigorous imprisonment, with Rs. 2,000/- (Rupees Two Thousand) fine,
and  in  the  event  of  non-payment  of  fine,  to  suffer  simple
imprisonment for three months. The same was upheld by the High
Court of Andhra Pradesh, at Amaravati, in Criminal Revision Case
No. 714 of 2010 vide the impugned order dated 26.11.2025.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that he is a tailor

--- Page 184 ---
2
by profession and whatever may have been recovered, i.e., two Rs.
100/- (Rupees One Hundred) notes, which are alleged to be fake and
recovered from him, were given to him by the customers whose
clothes he had stitched. It was submitted that in a village,
transactions, that too involving small amounts, are prevalent,
where cash is given, and in this case, being a tailor, neither does
he have the wherewithal to verify whether the notes are genuine or
fake nor, in view of the denomination being so low, i.e., two Rs.
100/- notes, the appellant could have suspected the same to be
fake.
5. Learned  counsel  submitted  that  in  the  present  case  the
appellant was not arrested at the first instance and only because
the co-accused, who was caught by the Police with fake notes,
disclosed that she was dealing in fake notes along with the
appellant, he has been roped in. Learned counsel submitted that
there were two other cases of similar nature which resulted in
acquittal.
6. Learned counsel submitted that the incident is of the year
2005, i.e., more than 21 years ago, and after 2006 there is no
other complaint against the appellant. Learned counsel submitted
that the conviction being under Section 489(C) of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860, which does not prescribe a minimum sentence, the Court
may show indulgence to him, and may consider modifying the sentence
to the period already undergone, which is 6 months, i.e., 180 days
of actual incarceration.

--- Page 185 ---
3
7. Learned counsel for the respondent-State submits that the
appellant was caught with two Rs. 100/- denomination notes, which
have been found to be fake and during trial, this fact has been
proved. However, she does not controvert the fact that after the
year 2006, there is no other case against the appellant.
8. Having considered the matter in its entirety and going through
the material on record, in the facts and circumstances of the
present case, we find that the cause of justice would be served if
the sentence of the appellant is reduced to the period already
undergone. We are informed that the fine has been paid by the
appellant.
9. Accordingly, the appeal is partly allowed. The conviction
recorded against the appellant is upheld. However, the sentence is
modified to the period already undergone. The appellant stands
discharged from the liabilities of his bail bonds.
10. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

Leave granted.
2. Admittedly, the writ petitions before the learned Single Judge
are  still  pending  for  adjudication  on  merits  regarding  the
alignment of the road, in which the decision of the Jaipur
Development Authority is under challenge. During the pendency of
the writ petitions before the learned Single Judge, directions were
issued as an interim measure to remove the constructions of the
appellants, which order was taken up in appeals before the Division
Bench. The Division Bench dismissed the appeals, resulting in the
filing of the present appeals.
3. In our considered view, once the writ petitions itself were
pending before the learned Single Judge for consideration on merits
regarding the alignment of the road in question, it was unjustified
of the learned Single Judge to have directed removal of the
constructions of the writ petitioners, i.e., the appellants herein.
The Division Bench also erred in dismissing the appeals.

shall maintain  status  quo  with regard to the constructions in
question.
6. Any observations made in the common impugned order shall not
influence the learned Single Judge in deciding the matter on its
merits in accordance with law.

[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated  14-07-2021

THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ORS.                 Petitioner(s)

BHAGWAN SINGH                                      Respondent(s)
IA No. 243658/2026 - CONDONATION OF DELAY IN FILING
IA No. 243663/2026 - CONDONATION OF DELAY IN REFILING /  CURING THE

IA No. 243661/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
 
Date : 18-09-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE PRASHANT KUMAR MISHRA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHREE CHANDRASHEKHAR
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Pashupathi Nath Razdan, AOR*
                   
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                              O R D E R
1. Learned  counsel  for  the  petitioners
would submit that the order passed by the
learned Single Judge is contrary to the law
laid down by this Court in the case of Union
of India and Ors. Versus Manju Arora and Anr.
(2022) 2 SCC 151  wherein, the following has
been held in paragraph nos. 17 and 19;

--- Page 213 ---
2
“17. We are quite certain that if a
regular promotion is offered but is refused
by the employee before becoming entitled to a
financial upgradation, she/he shall not be
entitled  to  financial  upgradation  only
because she has suffered stagnation. This is
because,  it  is  not  a  case  of  lack  of
promotional  opportunities  but  an  employee
opting to forfeit offered promotion, for her
own personal reasons. However, this vital
aspect was not appropriately appreciated by
the High Court while granting relief to the
employees.
19. In  the  above  circumstances,  we
find merit in the submissions made on behalf
of  the  appellants.  Consequently,  it  is
declared that the employees who have refused
the  offer  of  regular  promotion  are
disentitled  to  the  financial  upgradation
benefits envisaged under the OM dated 9-8-
1999.  In  this  situation,  the  Scottish
doctrine of “approbate and reprobate” springs
to  mind.  The  English  equivalent  of  the
doctrine was explained in Lissenden v. C.A.V.
Bosch Ltd. [Lissenden v. C.A.V. Bosch Ltd.,
1940 AC 412 (HL)] wherein Lord Atkin observed
at : (AC p. 429)
“… In cases where the doctrine does apply the
person  concerned  has  the  choice  of  two
rights, either of which he is at liberty to
adopt, but not both. Where the doctrine does
apply, if the person to whom the choice
belongs irrevocably and with knowledge adopts
the  one  he  cannot  afterwards  assert  the
other.”
The above doctrine is attracted to the
circumstances in this case. The employees
concerned  cannot  therefore  be  allowed  to
simultaneously approbate and reprobate, or to
put it colloquially, “eat their cake and have
it too”. It is declared accordingly for the
respondents in CAs Nos. 7027-28 of 2009.”

--- Page 214 ---
3
2. Issue notice  on  the  application(s)
seeking condonation of delay as also on the
Special Leave Petition(s).
3. In the meanwhile, operation and effect
of the impugned order(s) passed by the High
Court shall remain stayed.
         (NISHA KHULBEY)                          (POOJA KOHLI)
         COURT MASTER(SH)                        COURT MASTER(NSH)

Court in passing the common impugned Judgment and Order in WP
No. 2851/2026 & WP No. 3233/2026 respectively.
2. We take notice of the fact that the petitioner before us is the
original borrower. Since his account came to be declared as Non-
performing  Asset  (NPA),  Securitisation  and  Reconstruction  of
Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
(SARFAESI) proceedings were initiated. The secured asset was put to
auction by the Bank. The client of Mr. Neeraj Kishan Kaul, the
learned Senior counsel participated in the auction proceedings and
offered a bid of Rs.120 Crore. This bid was finally accepted by the
Bank. The sale has attained finality. All this happened in the year
2025. 
3. We also take notice of the fact that after the auction was
finalized, the petitioner moved an application under Section 17
before the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) with an application
seeking condonation of delay. The DRT declined to condone the
delay. Thereafter, an appeal was filed before the Debts Recovery
Appellate Tribunal (DRAT). The DRAT  entertained the appeal without
insisting for pre-deposit in accordance with Section 18 of the
SARFAESI Act. However, the Order passed by the DRAT did not find
favour with the High Court and that is how the common impugned
Judgment and Order came to be passed. 
4. We are informed that the liability of the petitioner - borrower
on the date of auction was Rs.46 Crore. Bank has been able to fetch

--- Page 217 ---
3
Rs.120 Crore in the auction. In such circumstances, the balance
amount of Rs.74 Crore subject to reconciliation shall be disbursed
in favour of the petitioner within a period of four weeks from
today.

Bank would submit that the balance amount has been secured by way
of a fixed deposit. If there is any other property owned by the
petitioner and the same has been attached by the Bank, the same
shall also be released immediately, if not yet released.  All
proceedings before the DRT or DRAT, if any, stand closed. The
question of law which has been raised in the present litigation as
regards the interpretation of the Second Proviso to Section 18 of
the SARFAESI Act is kept open.
6. In case of any further difficulty, the parties may come back
before us.
7. With the aforesaid, these petitions stand disposed of.
8. Pending applications, if any, shall also stand disposed of.

1. The served respondents are present in person. 
2. These  contempt  cases  were  instituted  alleging  willful
disobedience to the order dated 12.12.2025 passed by this
Court in Civil Appeal Nos. 14736-14737/2025.  By the said
order, the respondents in the appeals, viz. the authorities
of the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, were directed to
pay 89.19 lakh to the appellant therein, Manzoor Ahmad₹
Malik, the present petitioner, within a time frame.  
3. We are now informed that, though there was an issue with
regard to the required documentation contributing to some
delay, the sum of 78.04 lakhs has been remitted to the₹
account of the petitioner, Manzoor Ahmad Malik. This receipt
is acknowledged by the learned counsel for the petitioner. We
1

--- Page 225 ---
Cont. Pet. (C) Nos. 271-272/2026
are further informed that the sum of 11.149 lakhs has been₹
deducted, pursuant to Circular No. ET/ESTT/119/GST-SRO/2017
dated 21.07.2017 issued by the Finance Department of the
Government of Jammu and Kashmir, with regard to deduction of
tax at source under the J&K Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017.
4. In the light of the aforestated developments, we are of the
opinion that no case is made out for exercise of contempt
jurisdiction at this stage.
5. If the petitioner, Manzoor Ahmad Malik, has any grievance
with regard to the deduction of tax at source under the
aforestated Circular dated 21.07.2017, it is for him to seek
redressal thereof before the appropriate forum in accordance
with law.
6. Leaving it open to him to do so, the contempt cases are
closed.

We have heard Shri Jaideep Gupta, learned senior counsel
for the petitioner/State and Shri K.M. Nataraj, learned A.S.G
for the respondent(s)/Union of India and learned counsel for the
private respondents.
Between 15.12.2025 and today, what is of consequence is
there being a change in the State Government and formation of a
new State Government.
 Shri Jaideep Gupta, learned senior counsel contended
that the interim order dated 15.12.2025 has not yet been
complied with, firstly, owing to the change in the Government in
the State and secondly, that the talks between the State
Government and the Central Government though their Secretaries
have not resulted in any material consequence insofar as the
State Government is concerned.  He further submitted that an
application has been filed for recall of order dated 15.12.2025.
Be that as it may. We direct the petitioner/State to
comply with our order dated 15.12.2025 insofar as identification
of  the  requisite  extent  of  land  that  is  necessary  for
establishing Navodaya Vidyalaya in each of the districts of the
petitioner/State.

the said direction.  In the circumstances, we grant three
months’  time  to  the  State  Government  to  comply  with  the

of this special leave petition.
In  the  interregnum,  the  representatives  of  the
petitioner/State and the representatives of respondent Nos.2 and
3 to have a further dialogue with regard to the policy of
establishing Navodaya Vidyalaya in the petitioner/State.

that in the connected matters the component of interest has not

Psychotropics  Substances,  Act,  1985  and
sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a
period of 10 years and a fine of Rs.1,00,000/-.

criminal appeal against the conviction before
the High Court.  The appellant further filed an

 CRL.A. @ SLP(Crl) No.14555/2026 1

Court granted interim bail for a period of four
months  instead  of  suspending  the  sentence.
Aggrieved,  the  present  appeal  has  been
preferred.
5. Admittedly, the appellant has undergone more
than fifty per cent of the sentence awarded by
the Trial Court.

suspend the sentence of the appellant till the

to the effect that  the appellant’s sentence

                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Petition(s) for Special Leave to Appeal (C)  No(s).6769/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 10-07-2025
in WP No.31/2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay
at Goa]
STATE OF GOA & ORS.                                Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
SHANKAR CHANDRAKANT GAWAS & ANR.                   Respondent(s)
Date : 17-09-2026 This matter was called for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE AHSANUDDIN AMANULLAH
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE MANMOHAN 
For Petitioner(s)  Mr. Abhay Anil Anturkar, Adv.

                   Mr. Devesh Khandelwal, Adv.
                   Mr. Nishant Kumar, Adv.
                   Mr. Ankit Rana, Adv.
                                      
          
                             O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. The only issue left to be decided in the present case is as to
whether the respondent no.1 would be entitled for payment of
subsistence allowance during the period of his suspension i.e.,

--- Page 267 ---
2
from 19.02.2016 to 23.01.2025.
3. Learned  counsel  for  the  petitioners  submitted  that  upon
suspension of the respondent no.1, he never reported to the
authorities and one of the stipulations for payment of subsistence
allowance is that he should report and then, he should not leave
the headquarters without prior permission and further that a
certificate to the effect that he is not gainfully employed
anywhere else has to be furnished, which was not provided by the
respondent no.1.
4. Learned counsel for the respondent no.1 submits that due to
various reasons, some technical requirements may not have been
fulfilled but the basic right of respondent no.1 for subsistence
allowance cannot be just washed away or denied by the authorities
more so, because it is for the purpose of ensuring that the
delinquent and his family members are not left without any succour.
5. Having considered the matter, the undisputed facts remain that
the respondent no.1 was suspended on 19.02.2016 and he was arrested
by the Police on 29.03.2018. Thus, at least, on the day when he was
arrested, he was in the custody of the State. Thus, the obligation
to  pay  subsistence  allowance  would  lie  with  the  authorities
concerned.
6. Accordingly, direction is issued to the petitioners to pay the
subsistence  allowance,  as  may  be  admissible  in  law,  to  the
respondent no.1 from the date of his arrest i.e., 29.03.2018 till
the date his suspension was revoked. With regard to the intervening
period from the day he was suspended till the time of his arrest,
it shall be open to the respondent no.1 to move before the

--- Page 268 ---
3
appropriate forum in accordance with law, which shall be considered
on its own merits.
7. The  Special  Leave  Petition  stands  disposed  of  in  the
aforementioned terms.
8. With regard to such payment of subsistence allowance, whatever
formality which may be required, would be complied with/completed
by the respondent no.1 and if any ad hoc/lump-sum payment had been
made for the said period earlier, the same shall be adjusted by the
authorities concerned.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
(SAPNA BISHT)                                   (ANJALI PANWAR)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             ASSISTANT  REGISTRAR

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing for the parties.
The suit for specific performance preferred by
the respondent came to be decreed by the Trial Court.
The High Court, in first appeal, while confirming the

--- Page 273 ---
2
findings  of  the  Trial  Court,  exercised  its
discretionary jurisdiction with respect to a specific
portion of the suit property and directed respondents
to pay enhanced valuation to the petitioner.
     Aggrieved by the same, the present Special Leave
Petition  has  been  preferred  by  the  Petitioner-
defendant. 
Though the learned counsel appearing for the
petitioner made submissions on merits, we find that
the  consent  order  in  FAO  No.  307/2006  dated
21.12.2006, binds the parties. The report of the
Advocate Commissioner does indicate that the total
extent of suit property is 70.5 cents.
On a query, learned Senior Counsel appearing for
the respondent submits that a sum of Rs.1.76 crores,
in compliance of the judgment of the High Court, has
been deposited.
However,  we  find  that  the  matter  has  been
dragged on for a long time. We are dealing with an
agreement which was entered into in the year 2005.
Much water has flown under the bridge.
Though we are not inclined to interfere with the
impugned  order,  especially  in  the  teeth  of  the
earlier consent order passed by the High Court, the
interest of justice would be met if the sum of
Rs.1.76  crores  deposited  by  the  respondent  in
compliance with the judgment and decree of the High

--- Page 274 ---
3
Court is rounded off to Rs.2 crores. 
Accordingly, the remaining amount of Rs.24 lakhs
will have to be deposited by the respondent before
the lower Court within a period of four weeks from
the date of receipt of a copy of this order. 
On such deposit, permission is granted to the
petitioner to withdraw the amount. 
The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of,
accordingly.
However, we make it clear that the liberty is
given to the petitioner to withdraw the existing
amount already deposited, even before the compliance
of the present order is made by the respondent.
Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

Cont. Pet. (C) No. 468/2026
South East Central Railway, Ministry of Railways, Government of
India, is impleaded suo motu  as respondent No. 6 in this contempt
petition.  Issue notice to him, returnable on the next date.
We may note that the aforestated officer, despite the fact
that he is not a party to these contempt proceedings, has chosen to
file an affidavit on behalf of the named respondent No. 2 in the
contempt case.
The named respondents in a contempt case must speak for
themselves by filing their own affidavits instead of deputing their
subordinates to do so on their behalf. The matter is adjourned, to
enable  the  named  respondents,  including  the  newly  impleaded
respondent, to file their individual affidavits.  
We may also note that the affidavit filed on behalf of
respondent No. 2 by the newly impleaded respondent No. 6, speaks of
the sum of 61,67,430/-  (Rupees sixty one lakhs sixty seven₹
thousand four hundred thirty only) having been deposited with the
State authorities.  A detailed breakup of how the said amount was
arrived at shall be filed by the respondents concerned by the next
date of hearing.
Re-list on 16.10.2026.
Personal appearance of the respondents is dispensed with for
the present.

judgment today.
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Yashvardhan, Adv.
                   Mr. Apoorv Shukla, AOR
                   
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Ashutosh Kumar, Adv.
                   Mr. Arunava Mukherjee, AOR
                   Mr. Abhilosh Chaturvedi, Adv.
                   Mr. Kushagra Sharma, Adv.
                   Mr. Nisarg P. Khatri, Adv.
                                     
1. Hon’ble Mr. Justice Alok Aradhe pronounced the judgment of the
Bench comprising Hon’ble Mr. Justice Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha
and  His Lordship. 
2. Leave granted.
3. The  appeal  stands  disposed  of  in  terms  of  the  signed
reportable judgment. Paragraph nos. 44-47 of the Judgment read as
under:-
“CONCLUSION AND DIRECTIONS
44. We have referred to the asymmetry that exists
in our Country in the methods and manners by
which deposits are directed to be made before
Courts  and  Tribunals  in  appeals  which  are
considered. The asymmetry is reflected in many
aspects, and we have referred to some of them in

--- Page 466 ---
paragraphs 30 to 39 of our judgment. We have also
indicated  the  consequences  flowing  from  such
asymmetry and the compelling need to evolve a
normative  principle  that  would  apply  as  a
standard. We are of the opinion that it is
necessary to evolve and formulate a suitable
legislation on the subject.
45. We request the Law Commission of India to
examine the issues which we have highlighted and,
in the process, also consider the laws which
other countries have enacted. It may be necessary
for the Law Commission to consult the Reserve
Bank of India, Ministry of Finance and also the
Nodal Ministry of Law and Justice. 
46. The Registry is directed to send a copy of
our judgment to the Chairman, Law Commission of
India, Governor, Reserve Bank of India, and the
Secretaries to the Ministries of Finance and Law
and Justice.
47. However, in the facts and circumstances of
the case, we do not find any ground to interfere
with the impugned order. The same is hereby
affirmed.  With  the  aforesaid
observations/directions, the appeal is disposed
of.”
4.  Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

petitioners and the learned Senior counsel appearing for the
respondent.

High Court in the impugned order may not be sustained in the eyes

2
of the law, considering the peculiar facts of the case, we are
inclined to modify the same to the effect that the blacklisting

proportionality.

passed by the petitioner(s) will not stand as a bar for the
respondent to participate in other fresh tenders, starting from the
month of January, 2027.
The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of in the
above terms.

and trust that the  executing  court  will  make  all  efforts  to ensure  that the

dispute  between  the  parties  would  be  settled  by  arriving  at  an  amicable

judgment debtor(s) in the executing court would be granted some reasonable
time  to  quit,  vacate  and  handover  vacant  possession  of  the  suit  schedule
property to the respondent(s) – decree holder(s) or within such reasonable time
as may be agreed upon by the parties or as the executing court may deem fit to

                             O R D E R
1. This Writ Petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of
India, purportedly filed in the public interest, seeks to challenge
the constitutionality of:
(i) The Sikkim Private Universities (Establishment and Regulation)
Act, 2025; and
(ii) The Uttarakhand Private Universities Act, 2023.
2. In our considered opinion, the two statutes having been
enacted by two different State Legislatures, a common writ petition
assailing their validity would not be maintainable merely because
both legislatures have brought their respective enactments in
1

--- Page 794 ---
respect of a particular entry in the 2 nd List of the  Seventh
Schedule of the Constitution. Furthermore, an independent challenge
to each of the statutes can very well be instituted before the
respective jurisdictional High Courts.
3. We, therefore, dispose of this writ petition at this stage,
with liberty to the Petitioner to approach the jurisdictional High
Courts of Sikkim and Uttarakhand to challenge the subject statutes.
4. It is clarified that we have not expressed any opinion on the
merits of the matter, and the Petitioner shall be at liberty to
raise all the contentions before the respective High Courts.
5. The writ petition stands disposed of accordingly.
6. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 12-06-2026
in WPPIL No.13/2026 passed by the High Court of Gujarat at
Ahmedabad]
PALABHA NANGASHIBA                                 Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF GUJARAT & ORS.                            Respondent(s)
IA No. 270151/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE IMPUGNED
JUDGMENT, IA No. 270150/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
 
Date : 18-09-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) : Ms. Preetika Dwivedi, AOR
Mr. Abhisek M., Adv.
Mr. Ansh Rajauria, Adv.
                   
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner has assailed the impugned order passed by the
Gujarat  High  Court  dismissing  a  Public  Interest  Litigation
challenging  a  Government  Order  allotting  land  for  industrial
purposes under the Gujarat Agricultural Lands Ceiling Act, 1960 (in
short, the ‘Act’). 
2. It  is  contended  that  the  allotment  was  made  without
considering the scheme of priority envisaged in Section 29 of the
Act, and in violation of sub-section (5) thereof, which required
equivalent quantum of agricultural land of same class to be
1

--- Page 822 ---
surrendered. It is also contended that the High Court erred in not
entertaining the writ petition with reference to dismissal of an
earlier petition being Special Civil Application No.1788/2023,
wherein the petition had been dismissed on the ground of locus and
not on merits.
3. Though  the  arguments  at  the  first  blush  appears  to  be
attractive on the score that the dismissal of the prior proceeding
on a technical ground ought not stand in the way of entertaining of
the present public interest litigation, we have considered the
merits  of  the  matter  on  the  twin  premise  that  the  initial
government resolution to allot the land had been taken in 2022
(which remains unchallenged) and that the impugned allotment in
2025, substantially complies with the requirement of law vis-a-vis
quantum and quality of land surrendered by the allottee.
4. In these circumstances, we are not inclined to entertain this
Special Leave Petition. The same is, accordingly, dismissed.
5. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
